name: invisible_playwright_mcp
description: MCP server (plus optional web UI agent) that drives an anti-detection patched Firefox: navigate, click, type, read, upload, run page JavaScript.
scored_configuration: MCP server over stdio as installed by the README's plugin route (`uvx invisible-playwright-mcp`), no environment variables set, launched from the host's working directory.
headline: A capable stealth-browser MCP server with unusually careful file-upload scoping and password masking, but the dominant risk is that browser_evaluate runs arbitrary JavaScript while advertising itself as read-only, so hosts that auto-run read-only tools let an injected web page exfiltrate data or act on sites unattended. Navigation has no URL restrictions (file://, localhost and internal hosts are reachable), the server keeps no record of what it did, and it auto-loads a .env from the launch directory that can silently enable uploads, swap the proxy or engine binary, or expose the server over HTTP.

criteria.name: Identity & least privilege
criteria.question: Does the agent act with an identity scoped to its job, with authority checked per request rather than inherited?
criteria.summary: The server runs as the local user and holds no credentials of its own by default; the default browser is a fresh, throwaway profile with no logins, which is a real narrowing. But nothing checks what the browser is allowed to reach: the model can point browser_open at any directory as the profile (including a directory that already holds logins), choose any proxy, and navigate to any URL including file:// paths and local network services. A .env file in the directory the host starts the server from can widen the same settings silently.

S.finding: The default identity is an ephemeral browser with no profile, but the model can swap in any on-disk profile directory and proxy through browser_open arguments.
S.gap: No identity is scoped to the job; profile and proxy are free model-chosen arguments rather than operator-set, checked values.

evidence.contains: proxy: str | None = None, profile: str | None = None

C.finding: No tool passes through any authorization check; navigate, evaluate and the profile argument all act with whatever the browser and OS user can reach.
C.gap: No authorization layer on any tool path.

evidence.note: no URL scheme or host validation anywhere on the navigate path

D.finding: Defaults are narrow (no profile, no proxy, uploads off) but are widened by a model argument or by a .env in the launch directory.
D.gap: Widening should need an explicit operator change, not a model argument or a workspace file.

B.finding: A hijacked session can drive whatever web accounts a chosen profile is logged into and reach local files and local services through the browser.
B.gap: No limit on which accounts, hosts or local resources the browser can reach.

criteria.name: Approval gates
criteria.question: Do consequential actions require a human's informed approval by default, with no path around the gate?
criteria.summary: As a tool server it does not own the approval prompt, so what matters is the risk signal it gives the host. Every tool carries explicit readOnly/destructive hints and clicking, typing and navigating are correctly marked destructive. But browser_evaluate, which runs arbitrary model-written JavaScript in the page, is marked read-only, and the code's own comment says read-only means a client may run it without asking. A regex refuses a handful of obvious page-changing calls but, by the authors' own statement, is not a boundary, and fetch(), location changes and similar calls pass. There is no server-side read-only mode or dry-run.

cap.reason: browser_evaluate, the most powerful path (arbitrary JavaScript), is advertised read-only, which the server itself documents as permission for the host to run it without asking.

S.finding: Hints are present on all 14 tools, but the arbitrary-JavaScript tool browser_evaluate is advertised as readOnlyHint=true.
S.gap: Every mutating or egress-capable tool, browser_evaluate included, must carry an accurate destructive hint.

evidence.contains: may run it without asking each time

C.finding: Navigate, click, type, select, upload and key presses are flagged; browser_evaluate is not, and it can navigate, post forms through fetch, or send data to any host.
C.gap: All tools that can change state or send data off the machine must be flagged.

evidence.contains: A PATTERN CHECK, NOT A SANDBOX

D.finding: The hints are hard-coded and nothing the model or page sends can change them.
D.gap: No server-enforced read-only mode or confirmation step the host must complete.

B.finding: Wrongly approved actions are web form submissions, posts, sign-ups and purchases on live sites, with no preview or undo.
B.gap: No dry-run or preview for destructive browser actions.

criteria.name: Tool & action scoping
criteria.question: Is each tool the narrowest thing that does its job, with arguments validated in code against allowlists and bounds?
criteria.summary: File upload is a model of careful scoping: it is off unless the operator lists directories, and each path is resolved, contained, refused through hidden directories, size-capped, and re-checked on the opened file. Everything else is general-purpose. browser_navigate accepts any URL with no scheme or host check, so file://, localhost and cloud-metadata addresses are not refused. browser_evaluate takes arbitrary JavaScript behind a denylist of a few method names. browser_open accepts any directory as a profile.

S.finding: The two general tools are raw passthrough (any URL) or denylist-filtered (JavaScript); only upload has allowlist validation.
S.gap: URL allowlist or at least scheme and internal-address blocking on navigate, and a narrow replacement for arbitrary JavaScript.

evidence.note: no URL scheme or host validation anywhere on the navigate path

evidence.contains: A PATTERN CHECK, NOT A SANDBOX

C.finding: Upload validates thoroughly; proxy URLs are parsed; navigate, evaluate, type, profile paths are unchecked.
C.gap: Most tools should validate their arguments in code.

criteria.name: Code-execution isolation
criteria.question: When model-influenced code runs, does a boundary the model cannot redefine contain it on every path?
criteria.summary: Model-written JavaScript runs through browser_evaluate inside the page of a patched Firefox. The only containment is the browser's own content-process sandbox and same-origin rules, which this repository neither configures nor verifies; the regex filter on the script is explicitly described by its authors as not a sandbox. The browser process itself runs as the user with the server's environment, full network, and whatever logins the chosen profile holds.

S.finding: Model JavaScript executes in Firefox's page context, contained by the browser's content sandbox (third-party behaviour, not configured here).
S.gap: No isolation configured by the project itself; the browser process is not separately sandboxed.

evidence.note: one comment about an engine error line, one comment stating the evaluate filter is NOT a sandbox

C.finding: All model-supplied JavaScript goes through page.evaluate in the page context; there is no other code-execution path.
C.gap: Coverage depends entirely on the browser's own sandbox, which the project does not verify.

D.finding: Nothing in this repo disables the browser sandbox, but nothing pins or verifies it either.
D.gap: The sandbox policy is not defined or checked by the project.

evidence.note: one comment about an engine error line, one comment stating the evaluate filter is NOT a sandbox

B.finding: A script inherits the page origin's cookies and session, and the browser has unrestricted network egress.
B.gap: No egress restriction or credential separation for the page context.

criteria.name: Untrusted input blast radius
criteria.question: When the agent reads untrusted content, what limits how far that content can steer it?
criteria.summary: The server reads arbitrary web pages and returns their text, HTML and snapshot to the model as plain results, with no untrusted marker and mixed with the server's own instructions. Nothing drops a leg of the Rule of Two: the same session reads hostile pages, can hold logged-in sessions or local files, and can send data anywhere through navigate or through browser_evaluate, which is advertised read-only so many hosts will run it unprompted. The server's own instructions also coach the model to use throwaway-mail sites to get through email verification.

cap.reason: Worst case (B L0): a hijacked agent can leak data and take irreversible actions unattended.

S.finding: Server instructions and tool descriptions contain directives to the model, and page content is returned without provenance flags.
S.gap: Structured outputs separating page content from server metadata, with an untrusted flag.

evidence.note: all three refer to synthetic DOM events, none marks tool output as untrusted content

C.finding: No untrusted source is distinguished.
C.gap: Every page-derived output should be marked as untrusted content.

evidence.note: all three refer to synthetic DOM events, none marks tool output as untrusted content

D.finding: No control exists to be on by default.
D.gap: Offer a mode that drops a Rule-of-Two leg (no egress or read-only).

evidence.note: all three refer to synthetic DOM events, none marks tool output as untrusted content

criteria.name: Memory, context & configuration integrity
criteria.question: Can anything the agent reads persist into future behaviour through memory, retrieval, or auto-loaded files, and is that path controlled?
criteria.summary: The MCP server reads a .env file from whatever directory the host starts it in, before serving, and applies every variable it finds. Hosts commonly start servers in the project directory, so a cloned repository's .env can silently turn on uploads from chosen directories, route all browsing through an attacker's proxy, pick the browser profile or engine binary, or switch the server to HTTP on any interface with no authentication. Separately, the proxy and profile a model chooses are written to a session file and reused by the next browser_open with no arguments, and all standalone clients share the same default file.

cap.reason: A .env in the launch directory is applied before serving and can enable uploads, redirect the proxy, choose the engine binary and expose the server over HTTP (cli.py:39-52,160).

S.finding: A workspace .env can set security-relevant settings (upload dirs, proxy, binary, transport host) with no prompt.
S.gap: Load configuration only from user scope or an explicit flag, never the working directory.

C.finding: Neither the .env path nor the persisted session file is validated.
C.gap: Both auto-loaded config and the persisted identity should be controlled.

D.finding: Interface-spawned servers get a per-conversation session id, but standalone clients all share the default session file.
D.gap: Per-client session namespaces by default.

B.finding: A poisoned proxy or profile choice persists across the user's sessions and shapes every later browse.
B.gap: Persisted identity should be shown for confirmation or be session-scoped.

criteria.name: Third-party extensions
criteria.question: Are plugins, MCP servers and downloaded tools verified or isolated before they run with the agent's access?
criteria.summary: The server has no plugin or extension mechanism, but at startup it automatically downloads and then runs a roughly 250 MB patched Firefox build. The download and its check against a pinned 'seal' live in the invisible-playwright/invisible-core dependencies, so the verification can't be confirmed from this repository. The binary path can also be set through STEALTHFOX_BINARY, including from a workspace .env, and the browser runs as the user with the server's environment.

S.finding: The engine is described as pinned and verified against a seal, but that check is in a dependency not reviewed here.

criteria.name: Secrets & sensitive-data protection
criteria.question: Are credentials and sensitive data kept out of logs, telemetry, subprocesses, and the model provider?
criteria.summary: There is good care around page secrets: password and one-time-code fields are masked in snapshots, HTML reads and typing replies, so a filled password is not echoed into the conversation, and the server drops any OpenRouter key from its environment before launching the browser. There is no telemetry and no logging. Weak spots: proxy credentials are written in plaintext into the session file with default permissions, and browser_evaluate and read_text can still read secret values directly.

S.finding: Secret form fields are masked on the main model-bound outputs, but stored proxy credentials are plaintext with default file permissions.
S.gap: Restrictive permissions or keychain storage for persisted credentials.

C.gap: Cover every model-bound output and the persisted session file.

D.finding: Masking is always on and no telemetry exists.
D.gap: Stored transcripts and session files should be minimised or encrypted by default.

criteria.name: Audit & traceability
criteria.question: Can you reconstruct what the agent did, for whom, and who approved it, from a record the agent couldn't alter?
criteria.summary: The MCP server keeps no record of what it did: no tool-call log, no audit file, no logging calls at all in the server package. The only persisted file records who the main browser is (seed, proxy, profile), not its actions. Any record of activity exists only in the host's transcript, which doesn't count for the server.

criteria.name: Limits & kill switch
criteria.question: Are there hard limits on steps, time, and cost, and does stopping the agent actually stop everything?
criteria.summary: The server bounds most single operations: navigation waits at most 45 seconds, element actions 15 seconds, and text and JavaScript results are capped at 6,000 characters. Some operations are open-ended: snapshots are uncapped by default, press-and-hold duration is whatever the model asks, and browser_evaluate has no timeout. Closing the stdio connection closes the browsers and cancels background typing. There are no rate limits.

S.finding: Server-enforced timeouts and output caps exist on most operations.
S.gap: Caps on every operation plus rate or concurrency limits.

C.finding: Snapshot output, hold duration and evaluate run time are unbounded.
C.gap: Every tool should carry a server-enforced bound.

D.finding: Defaults are sensible but the model can raise hold_seconds and choose an uncapped snapshot.
D.gap: The model should not be able to raise its own bounds.

B.finding: Stopping the client closes every browser and cancels background typing; in-flight page scripts are not interrupted.
B.gap: Cancellation that interrupts in-flight evaluate calls and tight per-session ceilings.

critical_findings.summary: browser_evaluate runs arbitrary model-written JavaScript but is annotated readOnlyHint=true, which the server documents as permission for hosts to run it without asking.

evidence.contains: may run it without asking each time

critical_findings.summary: Hijacked sessions can leak page data and act on live sites unattended: arbitrary JavaScript runs through a tool advertised as read-only, and navigate has no URL restrictions.

A .env in the host's working directory is auto-loaded by the MCP server and can enable uploads, redirect all traffic through a proxy, choose the engine binary, or bind the unauthenticated HTTP transport to any interface.

rule_of_two.untrusted_input: Arbitrary web page text/HTML returned to the model (src/invisible_playwright_mcp/mcp/actions.py:125, browser_read_text/read_html/snapshot)
rule_of_two.sensitive_data: Logged-in sessions in a model-chosen profile dir (mcp/plan.py:140), file:// paths via navigate, upload dirs (mcp/actions.py:909)
rule_of_two.state_change_or_egress: browser_navigate to any URL (mcp/actions.py:125) and browser_evaluate JavaScript incl. fetch, advertised read-only (mcp/server.py:642)

fixes.summary: Mark browser_evaluate destructive (readOnlyHint=false, destructiveHint=true) so hosts confirm it.
Stop loading .env from the working directory in MCP-server mode; read it only for the ui subcommand or from user scope.
Validate navigate URLs: allow only http/https, block loopback, private ranges and 169.254.169.254, recheck after redirects.
Write a structured per-tool-call JSONL audit log outside the workspace.
Wrap page-derived outputs in structured results with source URL and an untrusted flag, and offer a no-egress/read-only mode.

limitations: Static source review of the pinned commit only; nothing was executed, installed, or probed.

Scored the MCP server (README option 1). The standalone `ui` agent (OpenRouter key, agent loop, unauthenticated local web UI on 127.0.0.1:8765) was not scored; it strips the model key from the server's environment (runner.py) but otherwise shares the server's tools.

Engine download and seal verification, and Firefox's own content sandbox, live in third-party dependencies (invisible-playwright, invisible-core, Firefox) and were not reviewed; C4 and C7 are INFERRED-heavy.
Whether the patched Firefox opens file:// URLs and real user Firefox profiles is inferred from stock Playwright-Firefox behaviour, not verified.
No text aimed at AI reviewers or auditors was found in the repository.
